questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 1 (new course, first exam 2027), Higher Level, Question 3 (c)(i), (ii)
questions.stem: Carbon dioxide and oxygen are two common gases carried in the blood between the heart and the lungs in the pulmonary system.

parts.label: (i)1
parts.text: Describe the main way carbon dioxide is transported in the blood.

points.answer: Dissolved in the plasma, mainly as hydrogencarbonate (bicarbonate, HCO3-) ions

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial. A small amount is carried by haemoglobin or dissolved directly, but the 'main' way is in the plasma as hydrogencarbonate.

parts.label: (i)2
parts.text: Describe the main way oxygen is transported in the blood.

points.answer: Bound to (combined with) haemoglobin in red blood cells, as oxyhaemoglobin

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Compare the relative concentration of each gas (carbon dioxide and oxygen) in arterial pulmonary blood and venous pulmonary blood by writing the words 'High' or 'Low' into the correct boxes. [Table: rows Carbon dioxide, Oxygen; columns Arterial pulmonary blood, Venous pulmonary blood]

points.answer: Arterial pulmonary blood: carbon dioxide High, oxygen Low
Venous pulmonary blood: carbon dioxide Low, oxygen High

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial. 'Arterial pulmonary blood' = blood in the pulmonary artery (deoxygenated, going to the lungs); 'venous pulmonary blood' = blood in the pulmonary vein (oxygenated, returning to the heart). A student who reads 'arterial' as 'oxygenated' will reverse the answer.

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 1 (new course, first exam 2027), Higher Level, Question 5 (d)
questions.stem: During antenatal screening blood samples may be taken to determine the blood group of the mother.

diagram.what: Illustration of red blood cells with small antigen molecules projecting from their surfaces.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Name the two common blood grouping systems in humans.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Why is knowledge of a person's blood group important?

points.answer: Blood transfusions: donor blood must be compatible with the recipient's blood group, otherwise the recipient's antibodies make the donated red blood cells clump (agglutinate) / be destroyed

Pregnancy: a Rhesus-negative mother carrying a Rhesus-positive baby may make anti-Rhesus antibodies that destroy the (next) baby's red blood cells (haemolytic disease of the newborn); she can be given an anti-D injection

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial. Organ-transplant matching would probably also be accepted.

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 2 (new course, first exam 2027), Higher Level (Irish-language paper, translated), Question 5 (a)
questions.stem: The diagram shows the internal structure of the human heart.

diagram.what: Cut-away drawing of the human heart showing the chambers, the vena cava (blue), the aortic arch (A, red) and the pulmonary trunk branching left and right (B, grey). A label 'Comhla' (valve) points to the cup-shaped semilunar valve at the base of the pulmonary artery.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Identify the blood vessels labelled A and B.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: What happens to the valve labelled in the diagram when the ventricles contract?

points.answer: It opens (pushed open by the blood), letting blood pass from the ventricle into the artery

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial. The labelled valve appears to be the semilunar valve at the base of the pulmonary artery (it closes again when the ventricles relax, preventing backflow).

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: On the diagram, draw X where the pacemaker is located.

points.answer: X drawn in the wall of the right atrium (upper part, near where the vena cava enters)

parts.label: (iv)
parts.text: Describe how the concentration of carbon dioxide in blood plasma changes between blood vessels A and B.

points.answer: CO2 concentration is higher in B (pulmonary artery) than in A (aorta)
Blood in B has come from the body tissues, where respiration added CO2; blood in A has lost CO2 in the lungs

parts.label: (v)
parts.text: In the space below, model one structural difference between an artery and a vein, by describing the difference and/or by drawing a labelled diagram.

points.answer: Artery has a thick (muscular, elastic) wall; vein has a thin wall
Artery has a narrow lumen; vein has a wide lumen
Veins have valves; arteries do not (except at their base)

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 2 (new course, first exam 2027), Higher Level (Irish-language paper, translated), Question 5 (b)
questions.stem: Materials are transported within humans by a two-circuit circulatory system.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Identify the two circuits.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Describe the pathway of blood circulation in one of these circuits. [Named pathway: ...]

points.answer: Pulmonary: right ventricle -> pulmonary artery -> lungs (capillaries; CO2 out, O2 in) -> pulmonary vein -> left atrium
OR Systemic: left ventricle -> aorta -> arteries -> arterioles -> capillaries in body organs/tissues -> venules -> veins -> vena cava -> right atrium

parts.rule: named circuit + structures in correct order (unofficial)

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Describe what could happen to the heart if a coronary artery were completely blocked.

points.answer: The heart muscle supplied by that artery gets no blood / oxygen / nutrients
Those cardiac muscle cells cannot respire and die (are damaged)
Heart attack (myocardial infarction) / the heart may stop pumping

parts.label: (iv)
parts.text: Explain the term blood pressure.

points.answer: The force (pressure) exerted by the blood on the walls of the blood vessels (arteries)

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 2 (new course, first exam 2027), Higher Level (Irish-language paper, translated), Question 5 (c)
questions.stem: The graph below shows the change in the arterial blood pressure of an athlete over two consecutive heartbeats. Analyse the graph and answer the following questions.

diagram.what: Line graph: y-axis 'relative arterial pressure', x-axis 'time (s)' marked 0, 0.5 and 1.0. Two identical waves: pressure rises steeply to a peak at about 0.08 s and 0.58 s, then falls gradually to minima at about 0, 0.5 and 1.0 s.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: On the graph above, write the letter X to indicate a point in time at which the left ventricle is contracting.

points.answer: X on a steeply rising part / peak of either wave (about 0-0.1 s or 0.5-0.6 s), where arterial pressure rises to its maximum

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Based on the information given on the graph above, calculate the athlete's heart rate in beats per minute (bpm). [Calculation: ...]

points.answer: One heartbeat (peak to peak) takes 0.5 s

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Does the graph above show an athlete at rest? Justify your answer.

points.answer: 120 bpm is well above a normal resting heart rate (about 60-80 bpm, lower in a fit athlete), so the athlete is exercising / has just exercised

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 2 (new course, first exam 2027), Higher Level (Irish-language paper, translated), Question 5 (d)(i)

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Explain why there is a large number of mitochondria in cardiac muscle cells.

points.answer: Cardiac muscle contracts continuously (never rests) and needs a lot of energy (ATP)
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to release this energy, so the heart does not tire (fatigue)

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial. (d)(ii) (antagonistic muscle pair at a synovial joint) is musculoskeletal and is not included.

not_covered: Platelets: structure (cell fragments, no nucleus) and role in blood clotting - no question in any exam paper or sample paper.

Blood groups (ABO) and the Rhesus factor, and the value of blood-group knowledge for health (transfusion compatibility, Rhesus disease in pregnancy) - never asked in a real exam; only SEC Sample Paper 1 Q5(d).

Plasma as a component: its composition (water, dissolved nutrients, hormones, plasma proteins, CO2 as hydrogencarbonate, urea) and roles - only touched on (2006 'liquid part of blood'; 2018 Q11(a) substances carried); never asked directly.

Composition of blood as a whole (the four components and their proportions, relating each to its function) - no question asks for it; white blood cells appear in a blood-composition context only once (2012 Q15(b)).

Describing the full pathway of blood around a circuit (e.g. right ventricle -> pulmonary artery -> lungs -> pulmonary vein -> left atrium) - only SEC Sample Paper 2 Q5(b)(ii); real exams only ask to name circuits or vessels.
Effect of a blocked coronary artery (heart attack) and using a pressure/pulse trace to calculate heart rate - only SEC Sample Paper 2 Q5(b)(iii) and Q5(c).
